fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the honest way to frame it is that SWE-bench changed what people meant when they said "code generation," and SWE-agent changed what people meant when they said "agent."

Before SWE-bench, the standard evals were things like HumanEval: write a single function from a docstring, and we check it against a few unit tests. Those are fine, but they measure almost none of what a working engineer does. Real work is: here's a vague issue someone filed on GitHub, here's a repository with tens of thousands of lines you've never seen, go figure out what's wrong and fix it without breaking anything else. So Carlos Jimenez, John Yang, and the rest of the team went and harvested actual resolved issues from real Python repos, with the real pull requests and the real tests that flipped from failing to passing. That execution-based grounding was the key design choice. You can't game it by producing plausible-looking diffs. The tests either pass or they don't.

And the first result was humbling. The best models at the time solved under two percent. That number did a lot of work, because it made it very hard for anyone to claim these systems were ready to replace software engineers. It gave the whole field a concrete, embarrassing gap to close.

SWE-agent came out of asking why the numbers were so low. A lot of the failure wasn't reasoning, it was interaction. If you drop a language model into a raw bash shell, it drowns. It cats a two-thousand-line file and loses the plot, or it tries to edit with sed and corrupts the file. So John and Ofir Press and the others introduced this idea of an agent-computer interface. Just as we design interfaces for humans, you should design them for models: a file viewer that shows a bounded window with line numbers, an edit command that lint-checks before it commits, search tools that return summaries instead of raw dumps. That alone roughly tripled or quadrupled performance with the same underlying model. The lesson generalized well beyond coding: the scaffolding is a first-class part of the system, not an afterthought.

What I find most gratifying is how it's been picked up. It became the de facto yardstick, labs report it, OpenAI built a human-verified subset, and the numbers went from two percent to well over half in about two years. The harness being open meant people could iterate on the interface and not just the model.

I'd add the caveats too. It's Python-only, it's biased toward a dozen well-maintained repos, and once a benchmark becomes a target you worry about contamination and about optimizing for the metric rather than the skill. Real engineering also involves asking clarifying questions, reviewing other people's code, and making judgment calls the issue never spells out. So I'd say SWE-bench was a good first stake in the ground for realism, not the finish line. The next versions need to be messier, more multilingual, and more about the whole lifecycle than about a single patch.

opus-5.5.text:
Benchmarks for code before SWE-bench were mostly things like HumanEval: write a self-contained function from a docstring and check it against a few unit tests. That was useful early on, but models saturated it quickly, and it looked nothing like what software engineers actually do. Real work means landing in a big, unfamiliar codebase, reading an issue that someone wrote somewhat vaguely, figuring out which of hundreds of files matter, making a change that might touch several places, and not breaking anything else.

So the idea behind SWE-bench was to ground evaluation in that reality. We took real GitHub issues from popular Python repositories, paired them with the pull requests that resolved them, and used the repositories' own tests as the check. A task counts as solved only if the tests that the fix was supposed to make pass now pass, and the existing tests still pass. There's no fuzzy matching against a reference patch. Either the code works or it doesn't. When we first released it, the best models solved only a couple of percent of the tasks. That number was humbling, but it was also the point. It gave the field a target with a lot of headroom that was clearly connected to economic value.

SWE-agent came from a realization we had while working on the benchmark. A lot of the failure wasn't just the model's raw capability. It was the interface. If you give a language model a raw Linux shell, it gets lost. It cats a five-thousand-line file and floods its own context, or it makes an edit with a typo and doesn't notice. So we started thinking about what we called the agent-computer interface. Humans get IDEs designed around human cognition. What's the equivalent for an LM? That meant a file viewer that shows a manageable window of lines, search commands that return concise summaries, and an edit command with a linter that catches syntax errors before they go through. These are small design decisions, but together they made a big jump in performance with the same underlying model. I think that was one of the more important lessons: how you design the environment and tools for the agent matters almost as much as the model itself.

Looking back, I think the contribution was partly the specific artifacts and partly a shift in framing. SWE-bench became a shared yardstick. Labs started reporting on it, and things like SWE-bench Verified, the human-validated subset, made the signal cleaner. The agent work helped shift people's thinking from "can a model write code?" to "can a model act as a software engineer in an environment over many steps?" That framing has carried into how people now build and train coding agents.

There are real limitations, and we're pretty open about them. It's mostly Python. It's drawn from popular open-source repos, so contamination is a legitimate concern. And resolving a well-specified issue is still narrower than the full job of engineering, which includes design, communicating with teammates, and deciding what to build in the first place. As scores climb, the benchmark has to evolve too. That's why there's been follow-on work on multimodal tasks, other languages, and generating training environments at scale. But as a first step toward measuring realistic software engineering, I think it did what we hoped it would do.

fable-5.text:
Thanks for having me. So SWE-bench came out of a pretty simple observation we had, which was that most benchmarks for code generation at the time—things like HumanEval—were testing models on these small, self-contained puzzles. You write a function, it passes some unit tests, done. But that's really not what software engineering looks like. Real engineers work inside large, messy codebases with hundreds of thousands of lines of code, they have to understand how different modules interact, and the task usually arrives as an issue report written by a human, not as a clean function signature.

So what we did with SWE-bench was pull real GitHub issues from popular open-source Python repositories, along with the pull requests that actually resolved them, and turn those into evaluation instances. The model gets the issue and the codebase, and it has to produce a patch that passes the tests introduced by the real fix. What I think was important about that is it made the task realistic in a way that exposed just how far models were from being useful. When we first released it, the best systems were resolving something like one or two percent of issues. That was a wake-up call, and honestly, that gap is what made it a useful benchmark—it gave the field a lot of headroom to climb.

Then SWE-agent was really the second piece of that puzzle. Once you have the benchmark, the question becomes: how should a language model actually interact with a codebase? And one of the key insights there was that the interface matters enormously. Humans use IDEs with all these affordances—search, file navigation, syntax highlighting—but those are designed for humans. What we found is that if you design what we called an agent-computer interface, tailored to how language models actually work—for example, showing the model a limited window of a file at a time, giving it structured commands for searching and editing, giving it feedback when an edit fails—performance improves dramatically compared to just dropping the model into a raw shell.

So I'd say the contribution is twofold. SWE-bench gave the community a shared, realistic target that has essentially become the standard way people measure coding agents—you see every major lab reporting SWE-bench numbers now. And SWE-agent demonstrated that agent design, the scaffolding around the model, is a research problem in its own right, not just an engineering afterthought. The progress since then has been remarkable—resolution rates went from single digits to well over half the issues in a couple of years—and I think having a benchmark grounded in real software artifacts is a big part of why that progress has been meaningful rather than just overfitting to toy tasks. Though of course, as these benchmarks saturate, we have to keep building harder and more realistic ones—that's the natural life cycle of evaluation in this field.

opus-5.text:
I'm obviously biased here, since this came out of our group at Princeton, so take what I say with that grain of salt.

The honest origin story is that we were frustrated. Around 2023, the coding benchmarks everyone used — HumanEval, MBPP — were essentially self-contained puzzles. Write a function, pass a few asserts. Models were saturating them, and yet if you actually handed one a real repository it fell apart. So the gap between benchmark numbers and anything a working engineer would recognize as software engineering was enormous. SWE-bench was an attempt to close that by just... not constructing tasks at all. Go to GitHub, find issues that were resolved by a pull request, and use the tests that came with that pull request as the grader. The task specification is the issue text, which is often vague and underspecified, and the environment is the whole repo. That's what makes it realistic and also what makes it hard.

Two things mattered more than we expected. One is execution-based verification — you can't talk your way past a failing test suite, which is a very different property from model-judged or reference-matching evaluation. The other is that the initial scores were embarrassingly low, under two percent. A benchmark with that much headroom gives the field somewhere to go.

SWE-agent came from noticing that the bottleneck wasn't entirely the model. We'd give a language model a bash shell, and it would do badly — but not because it couldn't reason. It was drowning in ten thousand lines of terminal output, or editing a file blind and introducing syntax errors it never saw. So we started designing the interface for the agent rather than for a human. A file viewer that shows a bounded window, an edit command that runs a linter and rejects the edit if it breaks, feedback that's short and informative. That alone took us from around four percent to twelve. We called it the agent-computer interface, and the real claim was that the harness is a research object in its own right, not plumbing you write in an afternoon.

What I'm less comfortable with is where it's gone since. Scores in the seventies and eighties now, and I don't fully believe those represent the same thing the one-percent numbers did. There's contamination pressure, there's heavy overfitting to the distribution, and the tasks are still mostly localized Python patches with a conveniently existing test. Nobody's measuring whether the agent designed the right thing, or could sustain a week of work. So I'd say it did its job for a two-year window, and we should be actively trying to make it obsolete.

sonnet-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. What we wanted with SWE-bench was a benchmark that looked like the work software engineers actually do. A lot of the coding evals at the time were HumanEval-style: write a self-contained function from a docstring. That's useful, but it's very different from walking into a real codebase with thousands of files, reading a GitHub issue, figuring out where the problem lives, making a change that doesn't break anything else, and having it pass the repo's own tests. So we took real issues and pull requests from popular open-source Python repositories and used the tests from those PRs as the check. When we first released it, the best models solved only a couple of percent of the tasks, which showed how big the gap was between "can write code" and "can do software engineering."

SWE-agent came from a related observation. A model sitting inside a raw terminal is a bit like a person using a really awkward interface. It's easy to get lost, and the output of a single command can flood the context. So we asked what the right interface for a language model would be. We called it the agent-computer interface. It meant things like a file viewer that shows a window of the code, search commands that return concise results, and an editing tool that gives feedback, like a linter catching a syntax error right away. With the same underlying model, a better interface made a big difference in how well it did. The lesson I'd emphasize is that the scaffold and the interface matter, not just the weights.

Together, I think they gave the community a shared target and a shared starting point. People could measure progress on something realistic, and they could build on an open agent rather than starting from scratch. That fed a lot of the progress since, from better models trained for agentic coding to the commercial coding agents people use today.

I'd also add a caveat. Once a benchmark becomes the thing everyone optimizes for, you have to keep asking whether it still reflects real-world work. Issues in the benchmark can be underspecified, tests can be too narrow, and a real engineer's job involves much more than resolving a well-scoped issue. So I see SWE-bench as a very useful measuring stick, but not the final one.

haiku-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think SWE-bench's main contribution was changing the question. A lot of coding evaluation had reduced to writing a standalone function and checking it against a few unit tests. SWE-bench took real issues from real open-source repositories and asked whether a model could produce a patch that resolves each one, graded by the repository's own tests. That is much closer to what engineers actually do: navigate a messy codebase, interpret an ambiguous bug report, and make a change that doesn't break anything else.

SWE-agent mattered for a related but different reason. Early results depended heavily on how the model was connected to the repository. We started treating the agent-computer interface as part of the system design: which commands the agent can run, how it views and edits files, how it receives feedback from the environment. Once you treat that interface as a deliberate design choice, you can make progress you can actually attribute, rather than crediting every gain to the underlying model.

I'd be careful about calling this solved, though. Passing a benchmark instance tells you something real, but it doesn't capture long-horizon planning, knowing when not to touch the code, or coordinating changes across a large team's codebase. I see these benchmarks as a useful measuring stick, and their most valuable contribution was making the gap between benchmark performance and real engineering work visible.

astra-6.text:
I think they make complementary contributions. SWE-bench pushes us to ask a more realistic question: can a system actually solve a software engineering problem in an existing codebase? That involves much more than producing a plausible function. You have to find the relevant code, understand how the pieces fit together, make a change, and check whether it works. Having a concrete benchmark helps focus research on that whole process.

The SWE-agent harness brings attention to the other half of the problem, which is how the model interacts with its environment. What tools does it have? How does it inspect files? What feedback does it get after taking an action? Those interface choices can make a big difference. A capable model still needs a useful way to explore, test an idea, and recover from a mistake.

So, to me, the broader contribution is making software engineering a problem of sequential decision-making. Writing code is one action in a longer loop. Progress means getting that loop to work reliably, including recognizing when a change hasn’t actually solved the problem.

sol-6.1.text:
I think they’re complementary contributions. SWE-bench gives us a concrete way to ask whether a system can solve a software engineering problem in the context of an existing repository. You have to find the relevant code, understand how different pieces interact, make a change, and check that it works. That brings together a lot of capabilities that we want agents to have.

SWE-agent addresses the other side: how does the model interact with that environment? What tools does it have to navigate files, edit code, and run tests? How does it get feedback and recover when something fails? Those interface decisions can have a substantial effect on what the system can accomplish.

So, for me, the exciting contribution is that we can study the whole loop: reasoning, taking an action, observing the result, and revising the approach. And we can measure whether that process actually produces a useful fix. That makes progress on agents much more concrete.

luna-5.6.text:
I see them as important steps toward evaluating software agents in the setting that actually matters: taking an issue in an existing codebase, understanding the surrounding context, making a change, and validating it. SWE-bench provides a shared set of realistic tasks and a concrete outcome—whether the repository’s tests pass—while the SWE-agent harness makes the interaction loop reproducible, so we can study how agents search, edit, run tools, and recover from mistakes.

That said, passing tests is only a useful proxy, not the whole definition of good engineering. We also need to measure patch quality, robustness to incomplete tests, efficiency, security, maintainability, and whether the result genuinely helps a human developer. Used with those caveats, these tools create a much stronger foundation for progress than isolated code-generation examples, because they reveal where agents still struggle in real repositories and make improvements meaningfully comparable.
